common_name: Bonnie and Mike Swamp White Oak (Beacon Columnar Swamp White Oak)

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in spring or fall in moist, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Bonnie and Mike is a tightly columnar swamp white oak selection discovered growing wild in Virginia's Shenandoah Valley, chosen for its narrow, stout-branched form that suits streets and other confined urban sites where the broad-spreading species would not fit.

directions: Plant in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in full sun, though this selection tolerates the periodic wet conditions and heavier clay that swamp white oak is known for in the wild. Bonnie and Mike was found as a naturally narrow, columnar specimen and has been propagated to preserve its stout upright branching and tight canopy, giving landscapers a swamp white oak option for boulevards, parking lot islands, and other confined urban plantings that could never accommodate the wide-spreading straight species. Growth is slower and more deliberate than typical swamp white oak, so allow extra establishment time and consistent watering through the first several seasons. Avoid highly alkaline soils, which can trigger chlorosis in this species just as it does in the species type, and expect the same glossy, two-toned foliage and yellow fall color once the tree matures.

common_name: Urban Pinnacle Bur Oak (Narrow Columnar Bur Oak, JFS-KW3)

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in spring or fall in average to clay soil in full sun; Urban Pinnacle is a patented upright-oval selection of native bur oak bred for street and small-lot use, with a strong central leader and smaller acorns than the wild species.

directions: Plant in average, clay, or compacted urban soil in full sun; bur oak is famous for its extreme adaptability, and Urban Pinnacle inherits the species' legendary drought and heat tolerance once its deep taproot is established. Selected from thousands of nursery-grown seedlings for its strong central leader and upright-oval crown, this cultivar keeps the tough, corky bark, fringed acorn caps, and coarse, glossy foliage of wild bur oak while fitting a far narrower footprint suited to streets and tight residential lots. Its leaves show good resistance to the powdery mildew and anthracnose that sometimes disfigure bur oak seedlings, and mature trees need very little supplemental care. Prune only to establish a single leader while the tree is young, since bur oak resents heavy pruning once established.
sources: J. Frank Schmidt & Son Co. nursery records

common_name: Independence American Elm (Disease-Tolerant American Liberty Elm)

planting.note: Plant nursery transplants in spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Independence was bred at the University of Wisconsin from resistant American elm parents and is the only patented member of the six-clone American Liberty multiclone developed to bring back the classic elm street tree.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, leaving ample room for the tree's dense, upright-vase crown to spread at maturity. Independence was bred by crossing especially disease-tolerant American elm selections and screened from thousands of seedlings, emerging as the sole patented clone within the American Liberty multiclonal release aimed at restoring elms to American streets. It shows good tolerance to Dutch elm disease, though like other American Liberty clones it remains more vulnerable to elm yellows, so growers in regions where that disease is active should monitor trees for yellowing foliage and premature leaf drop. Otherwise, Independence grows quickly into the graceful, arching silhouette that made American elm the classic shade tree for parks, campuses, and avenues before the disease epidemic. Water deeply while young and avoid wounding the bark, which can create entry points for disease-carrying beetles.
sources: USDA Forest Service Northern Research Station

common_name: Wynstar Willow Oak (Pyramidal Willow Oak, QPMTF)

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic soil in full sun; Wynstar is a broadly pyramidal, uniform selection of native willow oak bred for fast, dependable growth as a street and shade tree.

directions: Plant in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun, siting the tree where its broadly pyramidal crown can fill out into a dense, uniform canopy. Wynstar was selected for a more consistent, symmetrical habit than seedling-grown willow oak, retaining the species' fine-textured, willow-like foliage that emerges glossy dark green and turns shades of red, burgundy, and orange in fall. It grows quickly once established and shows good resistance to spider mites, a pest that can trouble willow oak in hot climates, while tolerating wet, poorly drained soils better than most upland oaks. Its smaller, rounder acorns provide reliable wildlife forage. Water regularly during the first two seasons and avoid alkaline soils, which can cause the iron chlorosis common to willow oak grown outside its preferred acidic range.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Toolbox
J. Frank Schmidt & Son Co. nursery records

common_name: Panache Shumard Oak (Broad-Pyramidal Shumard Oak, QSFTC)

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in spring or fall in rich, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun; Panache is an own-root Shumard oak clone selected for a uniform pyramidal-to-broad crown and dependable street and landscape performance.

directions: Plant in rich, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun, allowing plenty of room for the crown to broaden from a pyramidal youthful shape into a wide, rounded canopy at maturity. Panache was propagated on its own roots specifically to give architects and growers a consistent, predictable Shumard oak with glossy, deeply lobed dark green foliage that turns brilliant orange to red in fall, one of the most reliable red-oak-group fall colors in the South. It inherits the species' fast growth rate and strong tolerance of urban stresses such as heat, compacted soil, and drought once established, making it a popular substitute for pin oak in regions where soil pH causes chlorosis problems. Water deeply during the first two growing seasons, and prune only to correct co-dominant leaders while the tree is young.

planting.note: Plant nursery transplants in spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Delaware was selected in early USDA Dutch elm disease screening trials from among 35,000 inoculated seedlings and is one of the oldest disease-tolerant American elm clones still grown today.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Delaware forms a lower, broader crown than the classic vase-shaped American elm silhouette, so give it a wide planting area rather than a narrow street strip. Selected from a massive early USDA screening program that inoculated tens of thousands of seedlings with the Dutch elm disease fungus, Delaware proved to carry a fair, genuine level of resistance decades before more recently bred cultivars became available, and it remains an interesting historical choice for collectors and diverse municipal plantings today. It is notably resistant to elm leaf beetle, though like most older elm selections it remains susceptible to elm yellows, so plant it where that disease is not locally active. Water deeply during establishment and monitor periodically for early signs of disease, removing and destroying any infected wood promptly to protect nearby elms.
sources: USDA Forest Service Northern Research Station
